column2: On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Allah has pardoned my nation their mistakes, their forgetfulness and what they are coerced into.”
A ḥasan hadith, reported by Ibn Mājah, al-Bayhaqī and others.

Tajāwaza (“has pardoned”): has forgiven. “My nation”: the nation of response. Al-khaṭaʾ (“mistakes”): the opposite of what is right. Al-nisyān (“forgetfulness”): the opposite of remembering. “What they are coerced into”: what they are forced into against their will.

Allah the Exalted has pardoned the nation of Muḥammad ﷺ the sin of mistakes, forgetfulness and what they are coerced into; this is from Allah's kindness and mercy to His servants, the ease of His religion and the tolerance of the Islamic Sharīʿah.
One who forgets and one who makes a mistake are liable for damage and offences, because only the sin has been lifted.
What a coerced person carries out by force while under coercion does not take effect and is not concluded; rather, it remains as it was before the coercion.
This ease of pardon and forgiveness is particular to this nation.

This hadith contains great good news for the nation of Muḥammad ﷺ, for Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, has lifted the sin of a mistake—when what one did turned out other than what one intended—in something sinful,

the sin of forgetting after remembering, and the sin of what the servant is coerced into when he cannot find a way out of the coercion. Allah does not take [anyone] to account for these three matters, and this is from Allah's kindness and mercy to His servants in making the religion easy, with no hardship in it: “And He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship” [al-Ḥajj 22:78].
The printed text reads لشد فيه عسرفي, evidently for لا شدة فيه ولا عسر (“with no severity or hardship in it”).
O You who open for me every door that is hoped for, / I hope, my Lord, for Your pardon.
So bestow on me what brings about my happiness; / my happiness is to obey willingly whenever You command.
Every calamity, when it reaches its end, / is joined to a relief close at hand.
